question: What is CSRF and how does it work?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)** — Tricks an authenticated user's browser into making unauthorized requests to your site. The attack exploits the browser's automatic cookie attachment. Victims don't know they're making requests. Defense: CSRF tokens or SameSite cookie attribute.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of browser-based attack vectors distinct from XSS
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing CSRF with XSS — CSRF uses the victim's authenticated session, XSS injects scripts
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that CSRF attacks work WITHOUT JavaScript — a hidden form auto-submit is enough

sections.title: How CSRF Works
sections.content:
**Attack scenario:** 1. User logs into bank.com — browser stores session cookie 2. User visits evil.com in another tab 3. evil.com has: `` 4. Browser makes that GET request with the session cookie attached 5. bank.com processes the transfer as if the user initiated it **Why it works:** - Browsers automatically attach cookies to cross-origin requests to that domain - The server can't tell if the request came from the legitimate UI or evil.com - The victim doesn't know anything happened **For state-changing operations:** ```html
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- CSRF exploits automatic cookie attachment for cross-origin requests
- GET requests can be triggered by img/script tags — state changes must use POST
- POST forms can be submitted cross-origin with hidden auto-submit
- Defense: CSRF tokens (server-generated, unique per form) or SameSite cookies
- Stateless REST APIs with Bearer token auth are NOT vulnerable to CSRF
- Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default for web apps

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: CSRF tricks a victim's browser into making a request to your site without the victim knowing. The attack works because browsers automatically attach cookies to requests, including cross-origin ones. If the victim is logged into bank.com and visits evil.com, a hidden form on evil.com can POST to bank.com's transfer endpoint. The browser sends the request with the victim's session cookie attached — and bank.com processes it as a legitimate user action. The victim did nothing intentional. The two main defenses are CSRF tokens and the SameSite cookie attribute. CSRF tokens are unique per-session values that must be included in every state-changing request — an attacker on evil.com can't read your CSRF token due to Same Origin Policy. SameSite=Strict or Lax cookies don't attach to cross-site requests at all, which prevents the attack at the browser level.

sections.title: Speakable Answer v2
sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with OWASP-compliant security
sections.hook: CSRF is sneaky because the victim does nothing wrong — the browser does it for them.

beats.label: the exploit
beats.content: Imagine you're logged into bank.com. Your browser holds a session cookie. Now you open evil.com in another tab. That page has a hidden form that POSTs to bank.com/transfer. When the page loads, the form auto-submits. Your browser obediently attaches the bank.com session cookie to that cross-origin request. Bank.com sees a valid authenticated request and processes the transfer.

beats.label: two defenses
beats.content: CSRF tokens stop this by embedding a random secret value in every form. Attacker on evil.com can't read that value thanks to Same Origin Policy, so their forged form is missing the token and the server rejects it. The SameSite cookie attribute is a browser-level defense: SameSite=Strict means the cookie is never sent on cross-site requests at all.

beats.label: sharp edge
beats.content: sharp edge: CSRF doesn't require JavaScript. A plain HTML image tag like img src pointing at a state-changing GET endpoint is enough. That's why GET requests should never cause side effects.

question: How does a CSRF token work?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **CSRF token** — Server generates a unique random token per session, embeds it in forms/requests, and validates it on submission. An attacker on evil.com can't read the token (blocked by Same Origin Policy), so they can't include it in a forged request. Server rejects requests without valid tokens.

interviewer_intent.testing: CSRF defense mechanism understanding beyond just knowing the name
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking CSRF tokens need to be secret like passwords — they need to be unpredictable, not necessarily secret within the session
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the synchronizer token pattern vs double-submit cookie pattern

sections.title: CSRF Token Mechanism
sections.content:
**Synchronizer Token Pattern (Spring Security default):**
1. User loads a form
2. Spring generates random token, stores in HTTP session
3. Token is embedded as a hidden field in the form
4. User submits form — CSRF token included
5. Spring validates: token from form matches token in session
6. Attacker on evil.com can't read the token (Same Origin Policy) → forged request rejected

```html
<!-- Spring's auto-injected CSRF token in Thymeleaf -->
<form method="post" action="/transfer">
  <input type="hidden" th:name="${_csrf.parameterName}" th:value="${_csrf.token}">
  ...
</form>
```

**Double-Submit Cookie Pattern (for SPAs):**
- Token sent in both a cookie AND a request header
- Attacker can't set custom headers on cross-origin requests
- Used for REST-adjacent APIs

**Spring Security CSRF:**
```java
// Enabled by default for web apps
// Disable for stateless REST APIs:
http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());  // safe when using JWT
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- CSRF token: random per-session value embedded in forms
- Server validates token matches session — attacker can't read across origins
- Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default
- Disable for stateless REST APIs using Bearer tokens
- For SPAs: use the CSRF header approach (X-XSRF-TOKEN)
- GET requests shouldn't change state — CSRF applies to state-changing operations

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A CSRF token is a random value the server generates and ties to the user's session. When the user loads a form, the server embeds this token as a hidden field. When the form is submitted, the server checks: does the token in the form match the token stored in the session? If not, the request is rejected. The attack prevention relies on Same Origin Policy: an attacker's page on evil.com cannot read the CSRF token from your site's pages — it can submit a form but can't include the correct token. Spring Security implements this automatically for traditional web applications. For stateless REST APIs using JWT in the Authorization header, CSRF protection isn't needed and should be disabled — because the attacker can't forge the Authorization header across origins, only cookies.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with OWASP-compliant security
sections.hook: A CSRF token breaks the attack by adding a secret the attacker can't see.

beats.label: synchronizer token pattern
beats.content:
Here's how Spring Security's default approach works:
- User loads the form; Spring generates a random token and stores it in the session
- Token is embedded as a hidden field in the HTML form
- When the user submits, the token travels with the POST body
- Spring compares: token in request vs token in session
- They match — request allowed. They don't match — rejected
- Attacker on evil.com can't read your session token due to Same Origin Policy, so their forged form never has the right value

beats.label: spa variant
beats.content: For SPAs using AJAX, the double-submit cookie pattern works: the server sets the token in a readable cookie, the JavaScript reads it and adds it as a custom header (X-XSRF-TOKEN). Attackers can't forge custom headers on cross-origin requests.

beats.label: non-obvious
beats.content: non-obvious: the CSRF token doesn't need to be secret from the legitimate user. It just needs to be unguessable and unreadable cross-origin. The security comes from Same Origin Policy blocking evil.com from reading it.

question: Why are stateless REST APIs with JWT not vulnerable to CSRF?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **REST APIs and CSRF** — CSRF exploits automatic cookie attachment. If your API uses JWT in the Authorization header (not cookies), the browser doesn't automatically include it in cross-origin requests. Attacker can't forge the header cross-origin. Sessions in cookies = CSRF risk; JWT in headers = no CSRF risk.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of why authentication mechanism determines CSRF vulnerability
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Disabling CSRF for REST APIs without understanding why — should understand the reasoning
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the browser's cross-origin request behavior: cookies auto-attach, custom headers do not

sections.title: Why JWT Headers Beat CSRF
sections.content:
**Browser cross-origin behavior:**
- Cookies: browser automatically attaches them to cross-origin requests to that domain
- Authorization header: browser does NOT automatically add custom headers to cross-origin requests
- The Same Origin Policy blocks JavaScript from setting custom headers on cross-origin requests

**For cookie-based sessions:**
- evil.com's form POSTs to bank.com → browser attaches session cookie → CSRF works
- Server can't tell it's a forged request → CSRF token needed

**For JWT in Authorization header:**
- evil.com's form POSTs to api.example.com → NO Authorization header attached automatically
- Attacker would need JavaScript running on your domain to get the token
- But JavaScript on evil.com is blocked from reading your domain's data (CORS/SOP)
- Result: forged request arrives without Authorization header → 401, not processed

**Spring Security config:**
```java
http
  .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())  // safe for stateless JWT APIs
  .sessionManagement(sm -> sm
    .sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS));
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- CSRF works because cookies are auto-attached cross-origin
- Custom headers (Authorization: Bearer) are NOT auto-attached
- JWT in header = attacker can't include it in a forged request
- Disable CSRF in Spring Security for stateless JWT APIs
- HttpOnly cookies storing JWT: CSRF risk returns — use CSRF token OR SameSite=Strict
- SameSite=Strict cookie attribute also prevents CSRF even with cookies

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The key is how browsers handle cross-origin requests. For cookies, browsers automatically attach them to any request to that domain — even from another site. That's why CSRF works: evil.com can make your browser send a request to bank.com with your session cookie. But for custom headers like Authorization: Bearer, the browser does NOT automatically include them on cross-origin requests. JavaScript on evil.com is blocked from setting custom headers on cross-origin requests by the Same Origin Policy. So a forged request to my JWT API simply arrives without the Authorization header — my filter sees no token, returns 401, done. That's why I disable CSRF protection in Spring Security for stateless JWT REST APIs — it's not needed, and disabling it simplifies the configuration.

sections.title: Speakable Answer v2
sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with OWASP-compliant security
sections.hook: CSRF is a cookie problem. If your API doesn't use cookies for auth, the attack has nothing to exploit.

beats.label: why cookies are the problem
beats.content: Browsers automatically attach cookies to every request to a domain, even from a different site. That automatic behavior is what CSRF exploits. An attacker on evil.com triggers a request to your API and the browser helpfully sends along your session cookie.

beats.label: why jwt in headers is safe
beats.content: Custom headers like Authorization: Bearer are not auto-attached. Browsers don't add them to cross-origin requests. An attacker's form can POST to your API, but that request arrives with no Authorization header. Your JWT filter sees no token and returns 401. The forged request dies there.

beats.label: production trap
beats.content: production trap: if you store the JWT in an HttpOnly cookie instead of the Authorization header, CSRF risk comes back. The browser auto-attaches the cookie again. In that case re-enable CSRF protection or add SameSite=Strict to the cookie.

question: What is the SameSite cookie attribute and how does it prevent CSRF?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **SameSite cookie attribute** — Controls when cookies are sent on cross-site requests. SameSite=Strict: never on cross-site requests. SameSite=Lax: only on top-level navigation GETs. SameSite=None: always (requires Secure flag). Modern browsers default to Lax, which prevents most CSRF attacks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of modern browser-level CSRF defenses beyond traditional CSRF tokens
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that SameSite=Lax is now the browser default and its implications
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the security/usability tradeoff between Strict (maximum security, breaks cross-site links) and Lax (good protection, preserves links)

sections.title: SameSite Cookie Values
sections.content:
**SameSite=Strict:**
- Cookie never sent on any cross-site request
- Even clicking a link from evil.com to bank.com doesn't send the cookie (user appears logged out)
- Maximum security, worst UX — breaks "log in and redirect" flows
- Use for: highly sensitive operations, admin panels

**SameSite=Lax (default in modern browsers):**
- Cookie sent only on top-level navigation (clicking a link)
- NOT sent on cross-origin POST, AJAX, img, script requests
- Prevents CSRF for POST requests (most attacks)
- Allows: clicking a link from email/google results and being logged in
- Good balance of security and usability

**SameSite=None (legacy behavior):**
- Cookie sent on all cross-site requests
- Must be used with Secure flag
- Required for legitimate cross-site scenarios (embedded iframes, third-party auth)

**Spring Boot:**
```properties
server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=Strict
```
Or configure in SecurityConfig: `cookie.setSameSite("Strict")`

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- SameSite=Strict: no cross-site cookie sending — maximum security
- SameSite=Lax: no cross-site non-navigation requests — browser default, good protection
- SameSite=None: legacy behavior, must be combined with Secure
- Modern browsers default to Lax — better baseline CSRF protection for everyone
- Combine with CSRF tokens for defense in depth
- Spring Boot: configure in application.properties

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: SameSite is a cookie attribute that tells the browser when to include a cookie on cross-site requests. Strict means the cookie is never sent in cross-site requests at all — maximum security but it breaks some legitimate flows like clicking a link from an email and being automatically logged in. Lax, which is now the browser default, sends the cookie only on top-level navigations like clicking links, but not on cross-origin POST requests, AJAX, or embedded resource loads. That covers the majority of CSRF attacks. None is the old default behavior where cookies are sent everywhere — requires the Secure flag and is only for legitimate cross-site scenarios. For a Spring Boot application, I configure the session cookie with SameSite=Strict for the most sensitive applications, or rely on Lax for standard applications since it's the browser default.

sections.title: Speakable Answer v2
sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with OWASP-compliant security
sections.hook: SameSite tells your browser: don't automatically send this cookie to other sites. Three values, three levels of protection.

beats.label: three values
beats.content:
| Value | Cookie sent on cross-site? | Notes |
|-------|---------------------------|-------|
| Strict | Never | Max security, breaks cross-site link flows |
| Lax | Only top-level navigation (GET links) | Browser default, blocks most CSRF |
| None | Always | Requires Secure flag, legacy behavior |

beats.label: lax is the sweet spot
beats.content: Lax is the modern browser default and it handles most CSRF scenarios. It blocks cross-site POSTs, AJAX, and embedded requests — the primary CSRF attack vectors. It still allows someone to click a link in an email and land on your site while logged in, which is expected behavior.

beats.label: non-obvious
beats.content: non-obvious: because browsers now default to Lax, many apps get baseline CSRF protection for free without any config change. But you should still set it explicitly in Spring Boot with server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=Strict so behavior is guaranteed, not browser-dependent.

question: When should you disable CSRF protection in Spring Security?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **Disable CSRF when** — Your API is stateless and uses JWT or API key in Authorization header (not cookies). Enabling CSRF on a stateless REST API adds overhead without security benefit. Disable it: `http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())`. Never disable it for session-cookie-based web apps.

interviewer_intent.testing: Judgment about when rules apply vs when they're overhead
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Disabling CSRF for all projects because 'I read REST APIs should do this' without understanding the condition
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the exact condition: authentication mechanism determines CSRF relevance, not application type

sections.title: CSRF Disable Decision Framework
sections.content:
**Enable CSRF when:**
- Session-based authentication (Spring Security default sessions)
- Cookie-based JWT storage (token in cookie)
- Any case where cookies carry the authentication credential

**Disable CSRF when:**
- Stateless authentication: JWT in Authorization header, API keys in header
- Mobile app backends (no browsers, no CSRF risk)
- Machine-to-machine APIs (no human user sessions)

**Why it's safe to disable for JWT header auth:**
- Attackers can't forge Authorization headers cross-site
- No browser auto-attaches the JWT to cross-origin requests
- Every request authenticates itself via the JWT

**The right Spring Security config for JWT APIs:**
```java
@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())  // safe: stateless JWT
        .sessionManagement(sm -> sm
            .sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class);
    return http.build();
}```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Disable CSRF only when authentication is NOT cookie-based
- JWT in Authorization header = safe to disable CSRF
- Session cookies = keep CSRF enabled
- HttpOnly cookie storing JWT = keep CSRF enabled
- Always document WHY you disabled it — future maintainers need to know the condition
- Default Spring Security config has CSRF on — correct for web apps with sessions

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The decision depends on your authentication mechanism, not application type. If your API uses JWT in the Authorization header or API keys in headers, the browser never auto-attaches these to cross-site requests — CSRF attacks don't work, so CSRF protection adds overhead with no benefit. In that case, disable it with `http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())` and configure STATELESS session management. However, if your app uses session cookies — even if it's technically a REST API — CSRF protection is needed because attackers can forge requests with cookies attached. Same if you store JWT in an HttpOnly cookie instead of localStorage. The rule I follow: if cookies carry the authentication credential for humans in browsers, keep CSRF on. If all authentication flows through headers, disable it. And I always add a comment explaining why it's disabled so future maintainers understand the condition.

sections.title: Speakable Answer v2
sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with OWASP-compliant security
sections.hook: Disabling CSRF isn't about being a REST API. It's about how your authentication credential travels.

beats.label: disable when
beats.content: Disable CSRF when your API authenticates via the Authorization header — JWT Bearer tokens or API keys. Browsers don't auto-attach headers cross-site, so the CSRF attack vector doesn't exist. Also safe to disable for mobile backends and machine-to-machine APIs where no browser is involved.

beats.label: keep when
beats.content: Keep CSRF enabled when cookies carry the auth credential. That includes traditional session-based web apps and any setup where the JWT itself is stored in a cookie. The browser auto-attaches cookies regardless of origin, so the attack is possible and protection is needed.

beats.label: gotcha
beats.content: gotcha: many tutorials say 'disable CSRF for REST APIs' without the nuance. The correct rule is: disable when authentication is header-based. If you switch from JWT in header to JWT in cookie tomorrow, you must re-enable CSRF. Always leave a code comment explaining the condition.
